chapters.caption: Inside the Science Museum — five floors of the objects that built the modern world.
chapters.directions: From the entrance, head straight into the Energy Hall on the ground floor.
chapters.text: This museum exists because of a party — the greatest trade fair ever held. When the Great Exhibition of 1851 closed its glass doors in Hyde Park, it had made a handsome profit, and Prince Albert insisted the money buy land here in South Kensington and fill it with museums and colleges: 'Albertopolis,' Londoners called it. The science collections grew out of that Victorian shopping spree, became a museum in their own right, and moved into this grand East Block, opened in stages between 1919 and 1928. Today the Science Museum holds over 300,000 objects, and its genius is that the stars are not paintings or jewels but machines — the actual engines, capsules, computers and contraptions that dragged the world into modernity. A word on strategy before we dive in: this place is huge, five floors deep, and it rewards a plan. The ground floor is the historical spine — steam, industry, space — and it's where we'll spend our first hour. The upper floors hold the great themed galleries: medicine, flight, clocks, communications. Everything is free except the hands-on Wonderlab and the IMAX, so you can dip in and out of galleries as your energy allows. Start, as every visitor starts, surrounded by steam.
chapters.title: Welcome: A Museum Born of the Great Exhibition

chapters.caption: A Boulton & Watt beam engine — the partnership that put steam power into factories, mines and mills.
chapters.directions: Continue through the Energy Hall to the far end, where the gallery flows into Making the Modern World.
chapters.text: You enter the museum straight into its oldest and most atmospheric room: the Energy Hall, a cathedral of cast iron. Ranked around you are the beam engines that powered the Industrial Revolution, their great beams rocking — in their working lives — day and night, pumping mines dry, driving mill machinery and grinding corn. To understand what you're looking at, find the engines of Boulton and Watt. In 1712 Thomas Newcomen had built the first practical steam engine, but it devoured coal. James Watt's genius was the separate condenser, which made steam power efficient — and with his partner Matthew Boulton, who boasted that he sold 'what all the world desires to have: power,' Watt turned the engine into a product that factories queued to buy. Look for 'Old Bess,' an early Boulton & Watt engine of 1777, and the oldest surviving Watt beam engine in the world. Then find the strangest exhibit of all: Watt's attic workshop, recreated whole. When Watt died in 1819, his garret workshop at Heathfield Hall was locked up with everything in it — tools, models, half-finished experiments, even his tea things. When the house was demolished in 1927, the museum moved the entire room, all 8,300 objects, and rebuilt it here, dust and all. It's a time capsule of the mind that redesigned the world. As you leave, glance at the sheer scale of the later engines: within one lifetime, steam went from pumping a single mine to driving an empire's industry.
chapters.title: The Energy Hall: Steam Changes the World

chapters.caption: Puffing Billy (1813–14), the oldest surviving steam locomotive in the world.
chapters.directions: Making the Modern World runs along the ground floor; follow the timeline forward to the space age at the far end.
chapters.text: If you only see one gallery, make it this one. Making the Modern World lines up the museum's greatest hits along a single timeline, from the age of steam to the space age, and walking it is like fast-forwarding through 250 years. Start with the iron horse in front of you: Puffing Billy, built in 1813–14 by William Hedley to haul coal at Wylam Colliery near Newcastle. It's the oldest surviving steam locomotive in the world — a tubby, vertical-boilered pioneer that clanked along wooden and iron rails years before the railways proper began. This gallery was also the long-time home of Stephenson's Rocket of 1829, the winner of the Rainhill Trials and the template for every locomotive that followed; after nearly 160 years in London, Rocket moved in 2019 to its permanent home at the National Railway Museum in York, so consider this its empty plinth — the story is told here, the star now lives up north. Keep walking the timeline and the objects keep landing punches: the reconstruction of Crick and Watson's 1953 model of the double helix, built from metal plates and rods to crack the structure of DNA; a towering V-2 rocket, the first object to reach the edge of space, built as a weapon; early computers including the Pilot ACE, designed from Alan Turing's post-war plans. Slow down and read the labels — nearly everything here is the original, the first, or the only one.
chapters.title: Making the Modern World: Icons in a Line

chapters.caption: The Apollo 10 command module Charlie Brown, which orbited the Moon 31 times in May 1969.
chapters.directions: From Exploring Space, backtrack slightly and take the lifts or stairs up to Level 1 for Medicine: The Wellcome Galleries.
chapters.text: At the far end of the ground floor, the lights dim and the rockets appear. Exploring Space tells the story of how we left the planet, and its centrepiece is a scorched, conical capsule you could almost miss if you blink: the Apollo 10 command module, Charlie Brown. In May 1969, astronauts Thomas Stafford, John Young and Eugene Cernan flew this capsule to the Moon as the final dress rehearsal for Apollo 11. They orbited the Moon 31 times, and Stafford and Cernan took the lunar module Snoopy down to within about 15 kilometres of the surface — close enough to see their landing countrymen's future site — before firing back up to rejoin Young. Everything Apollo 11 did, Apollo 10 did first except land. Look closely at the heat shield's charred honeycomb: this capsule still holds the record for the fastest any humans have ever travelled, hitting 39,897 kilometres per hour on the way home. Around it, the gallery fills in the whole saga: early rockets, satellites hanging overhead, a full-size replica of the Apollo lunar lander standing in a pool of light, and the everyday spin-offs — from communications satellites to the technology in your phone — that spaceflight quietly delivered. Try the astronaut-glove challenge if it's free: doing up a bolt wearing pressurised gloves explains more about spacewalking than any label.
chapters.title: Exploring Space and the Apollo 10 Command Module

chapters.caption: Medicine: The Wellcome Galleries — five rooms and more than 3,000 objects on the story of health and healing.
chapters.directions: Cross Level 1 to the Information Age gallery on Level 2 — or ride up to Level 3 for Flight if aeroplanes are calling louder.
chapters.text: Upstairs, the tone changes from machines to bodies. Medicine: The Wellcome Galleries, opened in 2019, are among the largest medical displays in the world: five galleries and more than 3,000 objects tracing how humans have understood sickness and healing from ancient Egypt to the age of genome sequencing. Much of the raw material comes from one man's magnificent obsession. Henry Wellcome, the pharmaceutical magnate, spent a fortune collecting the entire material culture of medicine — and the results are gloriously eclectic. Keep your eyes open for two small objects with famous owners: Napoleon's toothbrush, ornate and silver-gilt, and Charles Darwin's walking stick, its handle carved as a skull — a memento mori its owner contemplated on his walks while evolution took shape in his head. Between those poles, the galleries do serious work beautifully: gleaming surgical instruments and prosthetic limbs that chart the craft of repair; the story of vaccination, antibiotics and the discovery of penicillin; diagnostic machines from early X-rays to the first MRI scanners; and contemporary art commissions that wrestle with what it means to be a patient now. Give this floor longer than you planned. It's the museum's newest masterpiece, and the one visitors most often say they underestimated.
chapters.title: Medicine: The Wellcome Galleries

chapters.caption: The Flight gallery — a hangar of full-size aircraft suspended three floors up, from biplanes to a Boeing 747 cross-section.
chapters.directions: From Flight, come down one floor to Level 2 for the Clockmakers' Museum and Information Age.
chapters.text: Now head up to Level 3 and walk into a hangar that has no business being inside a museum. The Flight gallery, first opened in 1963, packs full-size aircraft into the top of the building, suspended from the roof and stacked on the floor, so you walk in among wings, propellers and fuselages from the first half-century of powered flight. The star hangs near the centre: the Vickers Vimy in which John Alcock and Arthur Brown made the first non-stop crossing of the Atlantic in June 1919, flying 16 hours from Newfoundland to a bog in Ireland just eight years after... well, sixteen years after the Wright brothers first left the ground at all. Around it, find the fighters of the Second World War — a Supermarine Spitfire and a Hawker Hurricane, the pair that defended Britain in 1940 — and, poignantly, Amy Johnson's de Havilland Gipsy Moth, Jason, in which she flew solo from England to Australia in 1930, one of the great feats of the golden age of aviation. Don't miss the cross-section of a Boeing 747, sliced open so you can see how a jumbo jet is layered — seats, cargo, fuel and all — or the wall of aero engines showing how piston gave way to jet. Walk the gallery's length slowly and the story assembles itself: canvas and string to aluminium and jet fuel in under fifty years.
chapters.title: Flight: A Hangar in the Sky

chapters.caption: The Clockmakers' Museum — the world's oldest collection of clocks and watches, kept by the Clockmakers' Company since the 1630s.
chapters.directions: The Information Age gallery is on the same floor, Level 2 — look for the giant Rugby tuning coil.
chapters.text: Come down to Level 2 and step into the quietest, most jewel-like gallery in the museum. The Clockmakers' Museum is the oldest collection of clocks and watches in the world, assembled by the Worshipful Company of Clockmakers — the City of London guild chartered in 1631 to govern the trade — and on display here since 2015. Six hundred and more timepieces tick, chime and gleam in the cases, spanning five centuries. Start with the heavyweights: the movement of the Wells Cathedral clock, from around 1390, is among the oldest surviving clock mechanisms anywhere — a great iron frame of gears that once struck the hours for medieval Somerset. From there, watch precision become an obsession: the longcase clocks of Thomas Tompion, the father of English clockmaking; the marine timekeepers of the longitude era, when a clock that could survive a sea voyage and keep time to seconds was worth a fortune, because a ship's position depended on it; and the pocket watches that turned time into a personal possession. The gallery rewards slow looking — enamel dials, skeleton movements, watches made for queens and for railwaymen. In a museum of enormous machines, this room of small ones makes a lovely contrast, and it connects directly to our next stop: because once humanity could measure time exactly, it set about shrinking distance instead.
chapters.title: The Clockmakers' Museum: Five Centuries of Ticking

chapters.caption: Information Age — six networks that shrank the world, from the telegraph cable to the smartphone in your pocket.
chapters.directions: If Wonderlab is on your list, it's up on Level 3; otherwise begin drifting back toward the ground floor and the Wellcome Wing.
chapters.text: The Information Age gallery, here on Level 2, is built around a simple, brilliant idea: our connected world rests on six networks, and each gets its own island of objects. The Cable network begins with the Victorian internet — the telegraph — including sections of the first transatlantic cables and the equipment that let messages cross oceans in minutes instead of weeks. Broadcast brings Marconi's early wireless gear and the first televisions; the Exchange is a forest of telephone switchboards and Strowger switches that once clicked and clattered in every town; Constellation rises overhead with the satellites; the Web and the Cell bring the story to the smartphone in your pocket. The gallery's monument is impossible to miss: the Rugby Tuning Coil, a vast wooden lattice of copper wire from the 1920s long-wave transmitter that beamed signals across the British Empire — industrial cathedral meets radio set. This gallery has a royal footnote: it was opened in 2014 by Queen Elizabeth II, who marked the occasion by sending her first-ever tweet from the museum. Before you leave the floor, glance into the neighbouring Mathematics gallery, where a 1929 Handley Page aircraft hangs inside a flowing Zaha Hadid-designed landscape of equations — proof that even maths gets a blockbuster gallery in South Kensington.
chapters.title: Information Age: Six Networks That Shrunk the World

chapters.caption: Inside the Science Museum — five floors of galleries around the central hall; Wonderlab, the hands-on favourite, is up on Level 3.
chapters.directions: Exit through the Energy Hall; the Natural History Museum is next door on Exhibition Road, and South Kensington station is five minutes away.
chapters.text: If you're travelling with kids — or you're honest about being one — Wonderlab, up on Level 3, is the museum at play: a ticketed gallery of hands-on experiments with live science shows, a chemistry bar, giant slides that demonstrate friction, and a lightning demonstration crackling from a Tesla coil that you feel in your teeth. Book it ahead on busy days; it sells out. The Wellcome Wing, at the museum's west end, holds the IMAX cinema and the museum's big touring exhibitions, so check what's on — the Science Museum's special exhibitions are reliably excellent. And with that, our tour is done. Step back and consider what this building pulled off: in one visit you've stood beside the engine that industrialised the world, the locomotive age in embryo, the capsule that rehearsed the Moon landing, Napoleon's toothbrush and the coil that wired an empire. That's the Science Museum's argument, made in objects rather than words: the modern world wasn't inevitable — it was invented, piece by piece, by people whose actual tools are sitting in these rooms. If the day still has legs, the Natural History Museum is literally next door, and the Victoria and Albert is across the road. South Kensington may be the greatest museum neighbourhood on Earth. Enjoy it.
chapters.title: Wonderlab and Wrap-Up

intro: Welcome to the museum of how the modern world got made. The Science Museum tells the biggest story there is — steam, flight, space, medicine, computing — not with replicas and videos, but with the original machines: the oldest Watt engines, the world's oldest surviving locomotive, and a capsule that has actually been to the Moon. It's free, it's enormous, and it sits in the middle of South Kensington's museum quarter, a few steps from the Natural History Museum. This tour follows the route most visitors take: the ground-floor spine of steam and space first, then up through medicine, flight, clocks and communications. Give it a good two to three hours, and don't try to see everything — see the great things properly.

location.name: Science Museum, Exhibition Road, South Kensington, London

mapNote: Enter from Exhibition Road into the Energy Hall (Level 0). The ground floor runs east to west: Energy Hall, then Making the Modern World, then Exploring Space, with the Wellcome Wing and IMAX beyond. Medicine is on Level 1, Information Age and the Clockmakers' Museum on Level 2, Flight and Wonderlab on Level 3. Lifts and stairs sit at both ends of the building; work upward floor by floor and you'll never backtrack far.
practical: Entry is free, but book a free general admission ticket on the museum's website before you go — walk-up entry can mean a long queue at busy times.
Open daily 10:00–18:00, last entry 17:15; galleries begin closing from about 30 minutes before the museum closes.
Wonderlab, the IMAX cinema and special exhibitions are ticketed extras that often sell out on weekends — book those ahead.
Nearest Tube is South Kensington (Circle, District and Piccadilly lines); a pedestrian tunnel from the station runs straight to the museum quarter.
The ground floor (Energy Hall, Making the Modern World, Exploring Space) holds the biggest icons — if you're short on time, do that spine first.
There are cafés on several floors and a large shop by the exit; the museum is step-free throughout with lifts to every level.
subtitle: Steam engines, the Apollo 10 capsule, and 250 years of inventions that changed everything
title: The Science Museum
